stimulus_db: In ancient Greece, court witnesses were not cross-examined and the jury, selected from the citizenry, received no guidance on points of law; thus, it was extremely important for litigants to make a good impression on the jurors. For this reason, courtroom oratory by litigants is a good source of data on the common conceptions of morality held by the citizens of ancient Greece.
stem_db: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the argument?

choices_db.A: Litigants believed jurors were more likely to be impressed by litigants whose personality they preferred.
choices_db.B: Litigants believed jurors were more likely to subject the litigants' personal moral codes to close critical scrutiny than were people who did not sit on juries.
choices_db.C: Litigants believed jurors were likely to be impressed by litigants whose professed moral code most resembled their own.
choices_db.D: Litigants believed jurors to be more impressed by litigants who were of the same economic class as the jurors.
choices_db.E: Litigants believed jurors were likely to render their decisions based on a good understanding of the law.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: It was extremely important for litigants to make a good impression on the jurors.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Courtroom oratory by litigants is a good source of data on the common conceptions of morality held by the citizens of ancient Greece.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: The argument assumes that impressing the jurors was best accomplished by reflecting the common conceptions of morality held by the citizenry.

notes.body: Personality isn't morality. If jurors went by personality, the speeches would show what personalities jurors liked, not what the citizens believed was moral.

Close scrutiny of one’s moral code does not necessarily mean that the moral code was going to reflect the average citizen. It could be that litigants would profess an idealized moral code rather than one that accurately reflected the average citizen.

If litigants thought jurors favored people whose professed morals matched their own, litigants would shape their speeches to the jurors' morals. Jurors were ordinary citizens, so the speeches would reflect common moral views.

If jurors favored litigants of their own economic class, litigants would pitch their speeches to class, not to shared moral views. The oratory would then show what appealed to the jurors' class, which weakens the claim that it reflects common conceptions of morality.

If litigants expected jurors to decide on a good understanding of the law, they would argue the law rather than appeal to the jurors' morals. The speeches would then tell us less about common moral views, so E weakens the argument.
